topic: Natural Language Processing: Transformers, Attention, and Tokenization

questions.scenario: A legal tech company is building an automated contract analysis system processing long-form documents averaging 16,000 tokens. Using a standard Transformer architecture with standard Multi-Head Attention, the team observes quadratic memory footprint growth (O(N^2)) leading to Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors on 80GB A100 GPUs during inference. The system requires maintaining long-range context dependencies across multi-page agreements without simply truncating the text.
questions.question: Which architectural attention modification effectively addresses the O(N^2) time and memory complexity while retaining global document context?
options: A) Replace Multi-Head Attention with Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) and truncate sequences strictly at 4,096 tokens.
B) Implement a combination of Sliding Window Attention and task-specific Global Attention (e.g., Longformer architecture).
C) Increase the hidden dimension size (d_model) while proportionally reducing the number of total attention heads.
D) Transition from Post-Layer Normalization (Post-LN) to Pre-Layer Normalization (Pre-LN) in the Transformer encoder blocks.
questions.correct_answer_text: B) Implement a combination of Sliding Window Attention and task-specific Global Attention (e.g., Longformer architecture).
questions.explanation: Standard self-attention computes dot products between all pairs of tokens, resulting in O(N^2) memory and compute complexity with respect to sequence length N. Longformer reduces this complexity to O(N) by combining local sliding window attention (capturing local context) with selected global attention on specified tokens (e.g., document headers or key classification tokens), enabling the processing of 16k+ token documents without OOM errors.

questions.scenario: An enterprise e-commerce platform in India deploys a customer support chatbot to parse code-mixed Hinglish (Hindi-English) user queries containing frequent colloquialisms, slang, and typographical errors. The pre-trained WordPiece tokenizer trained primarily on formal English and standard Hindi splits short queries into excessively fragmented subword token sequences (e.g., a 6-word sentence gets fragmented into 26 subword tokens), causing severe inference latency and degraded downstream intent classification.
questions.question: Which strategy directly mitigates this over-segmentation issue and improves computational efficiency without retraining the core Transformer model from scratch?
options: A) Switch completely to character-level tokenization to eliminate unknown token [UNK] flags.
B) Extend the vocabulary with domain-specific Hinglish subword units using Byte-Fallback BPE and fine-tune the model's token embeddings.
C) Increase the maximum positional encoding capacity parameter (max_position_embeddings) from 512 to 2048.
D) Apply strict greedy decoding on character sequences prior to passing tokens to the embedding layer.
questions.correct_answer_text: B) Extend the vocabulary with domain-specific Hinglish subword units using Byte-Fallback BPE and fine-tune the model's token embeddings.
questions.explanation: Subword over-segmentation occurs when a tokenizer encounters out-of-distribution morphology or code-mixed text, breaking words into tiny, non-semantic fragments and inflating sequence length. By expanding the tokenizer's vocabulary with frequent domain/Hinglish subword tokens (using Byte-Fallback to handle rare characters gracefully) and fine-tuning the newly added token embeddings, the average sequence length decreases, directly reducing Transformer forward pass latency and preserving context.

questions.scenario: A financial news aggregator serving real-time market updates uses a 70B parameter Decoder-only Transformer model. During high-concurrency peak trading hours, GPU memory bandwidth becomes the primary bottleneck during autoregressive text generation due to the massive dynamic Key-Value (KV) cache allocation required for every active request thread, leading to SLA breaches in Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) and Time-Per-Output-Token (TPOT).
questions.question: Which structural attention optimization specifically targets and reduces the memory footprint and bandwidth bottleneck of the KV Cache during autoregressive decoding?
options: A) Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), which shares single key/value projection heads across groups of query heads.
B) Replacing Multi-Head Attention with Softmax-free Additive Attention (Bahdanau Attention) in decoder layers.
C) Switching from Absolute Learned Positional Embeddings to Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE).
D) Applying FlashAttention-2 algorithms exclusively during offline model training.
questions.correct_answer_text: A) Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), which shares single key/value projection heads across groups of query heads.
questions.explanation: In standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA), every query head has its own key and value head, creating a massive memory footprint for the KV cache retained per token in memory during autoregressive generation. Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) groups multiple query heads to share a single key/value head. This significantly reduces KV cache size (by 4x to 8x typically), relieving memory bandwidth constraints during inference and allowing significantly higher concurrency and lower latency.
